title: Debug and optimised builds
objectives: Compare debug and optimised builds, and know which one to time.

screens.title: Same source, two builds
screens.prose: A desk builds the tree benchmark from l9 twice from the same file, changing one flag. Illustrative numbers from a Linux server (Intel Xeon, 2.1 GHz, g++ 13.3), $n = 1{,}000$, median of five runs.
screens.question: How many times faster is the `-O2` build?

hints.text: Divide the slow time by the fast time.
Lines 3 and 6 hold the two times.

feedback.correct: Ten times faster, from one flag.

byKey.diff: 4.05 ms is the difference. The question asks for the ratio.
byKey.inv: 0.1 is the ratio upside down: slow over fast is 10.

explain.text: `-O0` asks for no optimisation: the compiler translates line by line and stores every value back to memory. `-O2` lets it rewrite the code while keeping what it computes. Same source, same prices, a tenth of the time.

screens.title: Which build to time
screens.prose: The same tree at all four optimisation levels, on the desk machine (illustrative, log scale). The desk's library ships built with `-O2`.
screens.question: Tap the bar a benchmark of the shipped library should report.

hints.text: A benchmark answers: how fast is what the desk actually runs?
The library ships with one of these flags.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which flag does the shipped library use?

byKey.o3: `-O3` is the fastest bar here, but the desk does not ship it. And `-O3` is not always faster than `-O2`: its bigger code can run slower on another loop.
byKey.o0: That is a **debug build**: right for stepping through code, ten times too slow to report.
byKey.o1: `-O1` is close here, but it is not what ships.

explain.text: A **debug build** (`-O0`) is for finding bugs; a **release build** (`-O2` or `-O3`) is what runs. Report the release build's time, and say which flags it used. This app compiles every exercise at one fixed level, `-O1`, so desk comparisons come from runs like these.

screens.title: One flag for each need
screens.prose:
A release build line on a desk might read:

```text
g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -g -DNDEBUG -Wall -Wextra -Werror pricer.cpp
```

Each flag answers one need. `-march=native` is one more: it uses every instruction this processor has, so the program may not run on an older one.
screens.question: Drag each flag to the need it answers.

slots.label: Names and line numbers for a debugger
Stop the build on any warning

hints.text: `-D` defines a macro. Which macro does `<cassert>` look for?
`-g` adds debug information; it does not change speed.
`-O2` speed, `-g` debugger, `-DNDEBUG` asserts off, `-Werror` warnings stop the build, `-march=native` this processor.

feedback.correct: Each flag does one job, and they combine.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read what each flag's letters stand for.

explain.text: `-g` and `-O2` combine: a fast build you can still debug. `-DNDEBUG` defines the macro `NDEBUG`, which makes every `assert` vanish. `-Werror` turns warnings into errors, so a suspicious line cannot slip through.

screens.title: What no flag can do
screens.prose: Level 2's American put checks early exercise at every node, calling `std::pow` twice per node: 1,000,000 calls at $n = 1{,}000$. On the desk, `-O2` priced it in 15.5 ms. Moving up one node multiplies the share price by $u/d = u^2$, so one `pow` per step is enough. The same `-O2` build then took 1.6 ms.
screens.question: Finish `american_put` without `pow` inside the inner loop. The tests check prices only.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and its first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Seven hidden tests: $n$ from 1 to 1,000, strikes £90 to £150 (deep in the money, where exercising at once is worth £50). Prices within a relative 1e-9 of the reference.

hints.text: Node $(i, j)$ has price $S u^j d^{i-j}$. What changes from $j$ to $j + 1$?
One more up and one fewer down: multiply by $u / d = u^2$.
Inside both loops: `node *= u * u;`. Before each step's inner loop: `node = s * std::pow(d, i);`.

feedback.correct: Same prices, about ten times faster on the desk: an algorithm change no flag makes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: At $n = 4$ the price should be 5.8828. Check each step starts from `s * std::pow(d, i)` and moves up by `u * u`.
byKey.test-6: Deep in the money the put is worth exercising now: £150 − £100 = £50. Check the early-exercise value uses the node's price.

explain.text: The optimiser must keep what `std::pow` returns exactly, so it cannot swap a million `pow` calls for repeated multiplication: the rounding would differ. You can, because you know the product is close enough. Rewriting the algorithm gave 10 times here; changing `-O2` to `-O3` gave nothing.

screens.title: An assert that stays on
screens.prose: `assert(cond)` from `<cassert>` stops the program with a message when `cond` is false. A build with `NDEBUG` defined deletes every assert. This app's build does not define `NDEBUG`, so here asserts stay on. With $n = 0$ the tree divides by zero and quietly returns a wrong number.
screens.question: Add asserts so `checked_call` stops when `n`, `sigma` or `t` is not positive.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and its first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Six hidden tests: two good inputs give the level 2 prices, and $n = 0$, $n = -5$, $\sigma = 0$ and $T = 0$ must each stop the program.

hints.text: One `assert` per input, before the pricer runs.
`assert(n > 0);`
`assert(n > 0); assert(sigma > 0); assert(t > 0);` then the return line.

feedback.correct: Bad inputs now stop loudly instead of pricing quietly wrong.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: With $n = 0$ the program ran to the end. Add `assert(n > 0);` before the return.
byKey.test-4: $\sigma = 0$ was not stopped. Assert on `sigma` too.
byKey.test-5: $T = 0$ was not stopped. Assert on `t` too.

explain.text: An assert states something that must be true for the code to be right. Here it catches a caller's mistake during testing. A release build with `-DNDEBUG` removes these checks, so inputs from outside the program need a check that stays, such as returning an error.

screens.title: The curve that never loaded
screens.question: Why does the release build print 0?

options.text: `-DNDEBUG` deletes the whole assert, including the call to `load_curve()`
`-O2` reordered the code, so the print ran before the load
options.why: Both builds use `-O2`, and the first prints 4. The optimiser never reorders away what a program prints. The only difference is `-DNDEBUG`.

options.text: The assert failed, and release builds hide failed asserts
options.why: Under `NDEBUG` the assert is not checked and fails nothing: its whole expression is gone, so `load_curve()` never runs.

options.text: The optimiser deleted `load_curve()` because its result was unused
options.why: `load_curve()` fills `curve`, a side effect the optimiser must keep. It was deleted by the preprocessor, before the optimiser saw it.

hints.text: Only one flag differs between the two builds.
Compare lines 1 and 3.
With `NDEBUG`, `assert(x)` expands to nothing at all, `x` included.

feedback.correct: Never put work inside an assert.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two build lines.

byKey.o2: You blamed `-O2`, but both builds use it. The difference is `-DNDEBUG`, which removes the assert and the call inside it.

explain.text:
With `NDEBUG` defined, `assert(expr)` becomes nothing, so any work inside it vanishes. Write `bool ok = load_curve();` then `assert(ok);`.

```cpp
bool ok = load_curve();   // always runs
assert(ok);               // only the check can vanish
```

canvas.caption: The release build never loaded the curve.

screens.title: Fast, but not maths
screens.prose: `-ffast-math` lets the compiler treat doubles like real numbers: it may reorder sums and assume no NaN or infinity exists. A quoting tool rejects a missing volatility, read as NaN, with `std::isnan(vol)`. The desk adds `-ffast-math` to speed it up.
screens.question: Should the pricing library be built with `-ffast-math`?

options.text: No: it can delete NaN checks and change results in the last digits, so tests and tolerances stop meaning what they say
Yes: it only makes arithmetic faster and never changes an answer
options.why: Line 4 shows it changed behaviour: the NaN check vanished. Reordered sums also change the last digits, which breaks reproducible prices.

options.text: Yes, as long as the tests pass in the debug build
options.why: The debug build has no `-ffast-math`, so its tests never see what the flag does.

options.text: No, because it makes the code slower
options.why: It usually makes code faster. The problem is that it changes the program's meaning.

hints.text: Read line 4: was the bad input rejected?
The NaN check stopped working.

feedback.correct: Pricing code keeps exact IEEE rules: no `-ffast-math`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read what the second build printed.

explain.text: Told that NaN cannot exist, the compiler decided `std::isnan(vol)` is always false and deleted the check. It may also add numbers in a different order, so a 10,000,000-term sum moved in its 12th digit on the desk. The tolerance reasoning of level 1 assumes IEEE rules; `-ffast-math` drops them.

screens.title: A check the optimiser deleted
screens.question: What happened in the `-O2` build?

options.text: Assuming `x + 1` cannot overflow, the compiler proved `x + 1 < x` false and replaced the check with `false`
The compiler has a bug: `-O2` must give the same answer as `-O0`
options.why: That holds only for programs without undefined behaviour. Overflowing an `int` breaks the rules, so no answer is wrong.

options.text: At `-O2` the addition wraps differently
options.why: No addition happens at all: the comparison was decided at compile time.

options.text: The `-O0` build is the wrong one: `INT_MAX + 1` is a large positive number
options.why: Neither build is right, because there is no right answer. Check before adding: `x == INT_MAX`.

hints.text: If overflow never happens, can `x + 1` ever be less than `x`?
The compiler may use 'overflow never happens' to simplify the comparison.

feedback.correct: Undefined behaviour lets the optimiser delete the very check meant to catch it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the compiler may assume about `x + 1`.

explain.text: For an `int` that never overflows, `x + 1 < x` is always false, so `-O2` returns `false` without adding. Test before the operation, `x == INT_MAX`, or use a wider type. Code that "works at `-O0`" may only be getting lucky.

screens.title: Which build is this app?
screens.prose: A program can ask how it was built. Compilers define `__OPTIMIZE__` at `-O1` and above, and `-DNDEBUG` defines `NDEBUG`. The starter already reports the first. This app compiles every exercise with `-std=c++17 -O1`, a level you cannot change, and leaves `NDEBUG` undefined.
screens.question: Add the `NDEBUG` check, using `#ifdef NDEBUG`, `#else` and `#endif`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and its first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs your program three times and compares what it prints, once character for character. The price line prints the same in any build; only the first two lines tell builds apart.

hints.text: Copy the shape of the `__OPTIMIZE__` block.
`#ifdef NDEBUG` is true when asserts are off.
`#ifdef NDEBUG` print "asserts: off", `#else` print "asserts: on", `#endif`.

feedback.correct: Optimised, asserts on: the price is the same as on the desk's builds.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare your output with the expected lines under the editor.

explain.text: The preprocessor picks one branch before compiling, so the program reports its own build. Here it is optimised (`-O1`) with asserts kept. The price, 10.4467, is identical at every level: flags change speed, never a correct program's answer.

screens.title: Test one build, time another
screens.prose:
What you have used, as a rule of thumb (CMake's build types, from the C++ course's CMake lesson):

```text
Debug           -g                 asserts on    tests, debugger
Release         -O3 -DNDEBUG       asserts off   benchmarks, desk
RelWithDebInfo  -O2 -g -DNDEBUG    asserts off   desk, with readable crashes
this app        -O1                asserts on    fixed
```
screens.question: Your tests pass in the Debug build. What should also happen before a release?

options.text: Run the same tests on the Release build too
Nothing: passing in Debug proves Release is correct
options.why: The overflow check and the assert with a side effect both behaved differently in the optimised or `NDEBUG` build.

options.text: Ship the Debug build, since that is the one tested
options.why: It is about ten times slower than release, and still the build the desk does not want.

options.text: Add `-ffast-math` to Release so it matches Debug's speed
options.why: That changes results and deletes NaN checks; it makes the two builds differ more.

hints.text: Which bugs in this lesson appeared only in the optimised or `NDEBUG` build?

feedback.correct: Test both builds; time the release build.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall the curve that never loaded.

explain.text: Undefined behaviour and asserts with side effects show up only in some builds. A CI matrix builds Debug and Release and runs the tests on both; benchmarks run on Release only.

screens.title: The desk's production build
screens.prose: The desk's pricing service runs all day. When it crashes overnight, the support team needs a stack trace with function names and line numbers, and the service must run at full speed.
screens.question: Which CMake build type should replace `???`?

options.text: `RelWithDebInfo`: `-O2 -g -DNDEBUG`
`Debug`: `-g`, so crashes are easy to read
options.why: Readable, but unoptimised: about ten times slower for the tree. `-g` can be added to an optimised build instead.

options.text: `Release`: `-O3 -DNDEBUG`
options.why: Fast, but with no `-g` a crash report shows addresses instead of function names and lines.

options.text: `MinSizeRel`: smallest binary
options.why: It optimises for size, not speed, and has no debug information either.

hints.text: You need two things at once: speed and readable crash reports.
`-g` and `-O2` combine freely.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which type has both `-O2` and `-g`?

explain.text: `RelWithDebInfo` builds at `-O2` with `-g`, so it runs at release speed and a crash names the function and line. A typical CI runs the tests on Debug and on `RelWithDebInfo`, and benchmarks only the second.

ideas: `-O0` is a debug build, about ten times slower on the tree; time and ship a release build (`-O2` or `-O3`), and say which.
`-DNDEBUG` deletes every `assert`, its expression included; `-ffast-math` drops IEEE rules, so pricing code avoids it.
Undefined behaviour lets the optimiser delete checks, so run the tests on Debug and Release. This app compiles at a fixed `-O1` with asserts on.

summary.trap: An `assert` with a side effect, such as `assert(load_curve())`, loses the side effect in a `-DNDEBUG` build.

quiz.prose:
```cpp
double total;            // never set
for (double p : pnl) total += p;
```
This prints the right P&L in a `-O0` build and nonsense at `-O2`.
quiz.question: What is the real bug?

options.text: `total` is never initialised: reading it is undefined, and `-O0` was lucky to find 0 there
`-O2` has a bug in its loop optimisation
options.why: The compiler is entitled to any value for an uninitialised `double`. Write `double total = 0;`.

options.text: The range-for loop skips the first element at `-O2`
options.why: Range-for visits every element at every level. The start value of `total` is the problem.

options.text: `-O2` turns on `-ffast-math`
options.why: `-O2` never implies `-ffast-math`; only `-Ofast` does.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What is `total` before the loop?

explain.text: An uninitialised local holds whatever was in that memory. At `-O0` that happened to be 0; at `-O2` it is a register with old data. `-Wall` warns about this, and `-Werror` would have stopped the build.

quiz.prose: A colleague says: "`-O3` always beats `-O2`, so always ship `-O3`."
quiz.question: What is the honest reply?

options.text: Often, not always: `-O3` makes bigger code that can run slower, so measure both on your own loops
Right: higher numbers always mean faster code
options.why: `-O3` unrolls and inlines more. Bigger code can miss the instruction cache and run slower.

options.text: Wrong: `-O3` changes results like `-ffast-math`
options.why: `-O3` keeps IEEE rules; correct programs give the same answers. Only speed and size change.

options.text: Wrong: `-O3` is always slower than `-O2`
options.why: On the desk's tree it was twice as fast. It depends on the loop.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Was `-O3` faster on the tree, and is that a law?

explain.text: On the desk's tree `-O3` took 0.2 ms against 0.45 ms, but on other code its extra unrolling and inlining can lose. Choose by measuring the real workload.

quiz.prose: You call `assert(n > 0)` with `n = 0` in this app's code widget.
quiz.question: What happens?

options.text: The program stops with an assertion message: the app's build keeps asserts
Nothing: the app builds with `-DNDEBUG`
options.why: The app compiles with `-std=c++17 -O1` and no `NDEBUG`, so asserts stay on.

options.text: It throws an exception the code can catch
options.why: A failed assert calls `abort`; it is not an exception. And this app cannot catch exceptions anyway.

options.text: The compiler refuses to build the code
options.why: The assert is checked when the program runs, not when it compiles.

feedback.correct: Asserts are on in this app.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what your build-report program printed.

explain.text: Your program printed "asserts: on": the app does not define `NDEBUG`. A failed assert prints the condition, file and line, then stops the program.

quiz.prose: A batch of 100,000 American puts at $n = 1{,}000$ took 15.5 ms each with `pow` at every node, and 1.6 ms each with one `pow` per step (both `-O2`).
quiz.question: How many seconds does the batch save per night?

feedback.correct: About 23 minutes a night from one algorithm change.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the saving per put by 100,000.

byKey.ms: 13.9 ms is the saving per put. Multiply by 100,000.
byKey.one: 1,550 s is the whole old batch, not the saving.

explain.text: $100{,}000 \times (15.5 - 1.6)$ ms $= 1{,}390{,}000$ ms $= 1{,}390$ s, about 23 minutes. Swapping `-O2` for `-O3` saved almost nothing on this loop.
